claim: Thirsty flies are motivated to seek a palatable source of water and to drink until they reach repletion.
source: Thirsty flies are motivated to seek a palatable source of water and to drink until they reach repletion (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A showing the thirst-induced sequence of behavior, and by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: A water source rapidly sets up a stable 3–6% humidity gradient from the edge to the source at the center of the chamber.
source: A water source rapidly sets up a stable 3–6% humidity gradient from the edge to the source at the center of the chamber.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the experimental setup.

claim: The longer flies are water deprived, the more quickly they find and occupy the water source.
source: The longer flies are water deprived, the more quickly they find and occupy the water source (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D demonstrating increased occupancy with longer water deprivation times.

claim: Water deprivation increases locomotor speed.
source: Water deprivation also increases locomotor speed (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1E showing increased speed with water deprivation.

claim: Thirsty flies seek water over food, and hungry flies seek food over water.
source: Given a choice, thirsty flies seek water over food, and hungry flies seek food over water, indicating that deprivation state-specific seeking can be readily measured in the open field assay (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by choice preference data in Figure 1F.

claim: Hygrosensory and taste cues guide thirsty flies to water.
source: A combination of hygrosensory and taste cues guide thirsty flies to water.
evidence: Supported by experiments manipulating sensory inputs (Figure 1G, 1H).

claim: Blocking access to the water source with a mesh grid had no effect on seeking.
source: Blocking access to the water source with the mesh grid had no effect on seeking, whereas removal of the third antennal segment that harbors hygrosensory neurons in the sacculus (antennectomy) reduced seeking (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1G.

claim: Removal of the third antennal segment that harbors hygrosensory neurons in the sacculus (antennectomy) reduced seeking.
source: Blocking access to the water source with the mesh grid had no effect on seeking, whereas removal of the third antennal segment that harbors hygrosensory neurons in the sacculus (antennectomy) reduced seeking (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1G.

claim: Combining antennectomy with the mesh grid completely blocked seeking.
source: Combining antennectomy with the mesh grid completely blocked seeking.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1G.

claim: Ablation of the aristae alone had no effect on seeking to the inaccessible water source.
source: Antennectomy also removes the aristae that sense temperature; ablation of the aristae alone had no effect on seeking to the inaccessible water source (Budelli et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Budelli et al., 2019.

claim: Water deprivation increased water intake.
source: Water deprivation increased water intake: removing the third antennal segment had no effect, whereas, as expected, blocking access with the mesh grid fully blocked intake (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1H.

claim: Removing the third antennal segment had no effect on water intake.
source: Water deprivation increased water intake: removing the third antennal segment had no effect, whereas, as expected, blocking access with the mesh grid fully blocked intake (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1H.

claim: Blocking access with the mesh grid fully blocked water intake.
source: Water deprivation increased water intake: removing the third antennal segment had no effect, whereas, as expected, blocking access with the mesh grid fully blocked intake (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1H.

claim: Thirsty flies use hygrosensory and taste environmental cues to locate and drink water.
source: Thus, thirsty flies use hygrosensory and taste environmental cues to locate and drink water, and we can isolate the hygrotactic water seeking step from other thirst-related behaviors.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the sensory manipulation experiments.

claim: The hygrotactic water seeking step can be isolated from other thirst-related behaviors.
source: Thus, thirsty flies use hygrosensory and taste environmental cues to locate and drink water, and we can isolate the hygrotactic water seeking step from other thirst-related behaviors.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental design using mesh grid.

claim: Durstig-Gal4 activation resulted in markedly high attraction to food.
source: One activation pattern, Durstig-Gal4 (the German for 'thirst'), resulted in markedly high attraction to food.
evidence: Supported by screening data in Figure 1I.

claim: Well fed, water replete Durstig>TrpA1 flies avidly occupied standard fly food, wet sucrose or yeast alone in 1% agar, dry sucrose, 1% agar alone, or water alone.
source: Well fed, water replete Durstig>TrpA1 flies avidly occupied standard fly food, wet sucrose or yeast alone in 1% agar, dry sucrose, 1% agar alone, or water alone, but they were not attracted to empty receptacles (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1J.

claim: Durstig>TrpA1 flies were not attracted to empty receptacles.
source: Well fed, water replete Durstig>TrpA1 flies avidly occupied standard fly food, wet sucrose or yeast alone in 1% agar, dry sucrose, 1% agar alone, or water alone, but they were not attracted to empty receptacles (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1J.

claim: Hygrotaxis toward inaccessible water was strongly potentiated by Durstig activation.
source: Hygrotaxis toward inaccessible water was strongly potentiated by Durstig activation (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1K.

claim: Durstig contains neurons that promote water seeking.
source: Thus, Durstig contains neurons that promote water seeking.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the Durstig activation experiments.

claim: Activation of dopamine neurons for reward and aversion had either no effect or suppressed water seeking.
source: Activation of dopamine neurons for reward and aversion had either no effect or suppressed water seeking (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons previously implicated in humidity preference and water reward, in the R48B04 pattern, are different from the Durstig water seeking neurons.
source: Moreover, dopaminergic neurons previously implicated in humidity preference and water reward, in the R48B04 pattern, are different from the Durstig water seeking neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by genetic subtraction experiments in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Activation of the NP883 pattern containing the Fdg neurons that promote proboscis extension and liquid food intake increased water seeking.
source: Of neurons implicated in feeding, activation of only two patterns increased water seeking: the NP883 pattern containing the Fdg neurons that promote proboscis extension and liquid food intake, and the R65D05 pattern that contains AstA neurons that inhibit food intake (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Chen et al., 2016; Flood et al., 2013; Hentze et al., 2015; Hergarden et al., 2012; Pool et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and citations.

claim: Activation of the R65D05 pattern that contains AstA neurons that inhibit food intake increased water seeking.
source: Of neurons implicated in feeding, activation of only two patterns increased water seeking: the NP883 pattern containing the Fdg neurons that promote proboscis extension and liquid food intake, and the R65D05 pattern that contains AstA neurons that inhibit food intake (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Chen et al., 2016; Flood et al., 2013; Hentze et al., 2015; Hergarden et al., 2012; Pool et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and citations.

claim: Activation of internal osmosensory ISNs (R34G02), hygrosensory neurons (Ir40a, Ir68a), and water taste neurons (ppk28) did not increase water seeking.
source: Activation of internal osmosensory ISNs (R34G02), hygrosensory neurons (Ir40a, Ir68a), and water taste neurons (ppk28) did not increase water seeking (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D; Enjin et al., 2016; Jourjine et al., 2016; Knecht et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and citations.

claim: There is segregation of water seeking from many of the previously identified neurons involved in steps of feeding and intake.
source: These findings reveal segregation of water seeking from many of the previously identified neurons involved in steps of feeding and intake.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the activation screen results.

claim: Subtracting R65D05 neurons from Durstig reduced activation-dependent water seeking.
source: First, subtracting R65D05 neurons from Durstig reduced activation-dependent water seeking, indicating that the water seeking neurons in Durstig and R65D05 are the same (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by genetic subtraction experiments in Figure 2A.

claim: The water seeking neurons in Durstig and R65D05 are the same.
source: First, subtracting R65D05 neurons from Durstig reduced activation-dependent water seeking, indicating that the water seeking neurons in Durstig and R65D05 are the same (Figure 2A).
evidence: Inferred from the genetic subtraction experiment results.

claim: Activation of central brain R65D05 neurons promoted water seeking.
source: Activation of central brain R65D05 neurons promoted water seeking, whereas their inactivation decreased seeking, indicating that central brain neurons in the R65D05 pattern (and not ventral nervous system neurons or other non-neuronal cells) are both necessary and sufficient for water seeking (Figure 2B,C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: Inactivation of central brain R65D05 neurons decreased water seeking.
source: Activation of central brain R65D05 neurons promoted water seeking, whereas their inactivation decreased seeking, indicating that central brain neurons in the R65D05 pattern (and not ventral nervous system neurons or other non-neuronal cells) are both necessary and sufficient for water seeking (Figure 2B,C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: Central brain neurons in the R65D05 pattern are both necessary and sufficient for water seeking.
source: Activation of central brain R65D05 neurons promoted water seeking, whereas their inactivation decreased seeking, indicating that central brain neurons in the R65D05 pattern (and not ventral nervous system neurons or other non-neuronal cells) are both necessary and sufficient for water seeking (Figure 2B,C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from activation and inactivation experiments.

claim: Feeding behavior toward dry sucrose was increased with R65D05 inactivation.
source: Feeding behavior toward dry sucrose was increased with R65D05 inactivation, as expected from previous reports (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F; Chen et al., 2016; Hentze et al., 2015; Hergarden et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and citations.

claim: Subtracting out neurons with VGlut-Gal80 specifically suppressed Durstig water seeking.
source: Second, we expressed the GAL4 inhibitor GAL80 in various neurotransmitter classes of neurons and assessed Durstig activation-driven water seeking. Subtracting out neurons with VGlut-Gal80 (vesicular glutamate transporter enhancer) specifically suppressed Durstig water seeking (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: R52A01-Gal4 neurons are able to promote water seeking.
source: Next, we activated neurons captured by enhancer-Gal4 transgenes created with enhancer fragments taken from the VGlut locus, and we identified R52A01-Gal4 neurons as being able to promote water seeking (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Subtracting R52A01 neurons from the Durstig pattern blocked Durstig activation from increasing water seeking.
source: Subtracting R52A01 neurons from the Durstig pattern blocked Durstig activation from increasing water seeking, indicating that Durstig water seeking neurons were also found in R52A01 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by genetic subtraction experiments in Figure 2D.

claim: Durstig water seeking neurons were also found in R52A01.
source: Subtracting R52A01 neurons from the Durstig pattern blocked Durstig activation from increasing water seeking, indicating that Durstig water seeking neurons were also found in R52A01 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Inferred from the genetic subtraction experiment results.

claim: R52A01 activation increased water seeking.
source: Like R65D05, R52A01 activation increased and R52A01 inhibition decreased water seeking (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2E,F.

claim: R52A01 inhibition decreased water seeking.
source: Like R65D05, R52A01 activation increased and R52A01 inhibition decreased water seeking (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Subtracting out neurons with VGlut-Gal80 decreased thirsty water seeking in both TrpA1-activated R52A01 and R65D05.
source: Subtracting out neurons with VGlut-Gal80 decreased thirsty water seeking in both TrpA1-activated R52A01 and R65D05, suggesting that the water seeking neurons were shared between these two Gal4 driver transgenes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E,F.

claim: The water seeking neurons were shared between R52A01 and R65D05 Gal4 driver transgenes.
source: Subtracting out neurons with VGlut-Gal80 decreased thirsty water seeking in both TrpA1-activated R52A01 and R65D05, suggesting that the water seeking neurons were shared between these two Gal4 driver transgenes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: Inferred from the VGlut-Gal80 subtraction experiments.

claim: Janu-spGal4 is expressed in four bilaterally symmetric neurons in the central brain.
source: Janu-spGal4 is expressed in four bilaterally symmetric neurons in the central brain (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data in Figure 2H.

claim: Janu neuron postsynaptic inputs are confined to the subesophageal zone (SEZ).
source: Janu neuron postsynaptic inputs are confined to the subesophageal zone (SEZ), and their presynaptic outputs are distributed between the SEZ, the crepine region (CRE), and the superior medial protocerebrum (SMP) (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data in Figure 2I.

claim: Janu neuron presynaptic outputs are distributed between the SEZ, the crepine region (CRE), and the superior medial protocerebrum (SMP).
source: Janu neuron postsynaptic inputs are confined to the subesophageal zone (SEZ), and their presynaptic outputs are distributed between the SEZ, the crepine region (CRE), and the superior medial protocerebrum (SMP) (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data in Figure 2I.

claim: TrpA1 activation of Janu neurons increased water seeking.
source: TrpA1 activation of Janu neurons increased water seeking, albeit to a lesser extent than either parental Gal4 driver alone (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2J.

claim: Acute inactivation of Janu neurons decreased thirsty water seeking.
source: Conversely, acute inactivation of Janu neurons decreased thirsty water seeking (Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2K.

claim: The behavioral effects of both Janu activation and inactivation on water seeking mapped to the central brain.
source: The behavioral effects of both Janu activation and inactivation on water seeking mapped to the central brain, similar to the parental enhancer-Gal4s for Janu-spGal4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: Feeding behavior was increased when Janu neurons were acutely inactivated.
source: Interestingly, feeding behavior was increased when Janu neurons were acutely inactivated, the opposite effect as compared to water seeking (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D,E.

claim: The Janu neurons promote water seeking and inhibit feeding behavior.
source: Thus, the Janu neurons promote water seeking and inhibit feeding behavior.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the activation and inactivation experiments.

claim: Two of the four central brain Janu neurons project locally in the SEZ.
source: Two of the four central brain Janu neurons project locally in the SEZ, and the other two neurons project from the SEZ to the CRE and/or the SMP.
evidence: Supported by stochastic labeling data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Two of the four central brain Janu neurons project from the SEZ to the CRE and/or the SMP.
source: Two of the four central brain Janu neurons project locally in the SEZ, and the other two neurons project from the SEZ to the CRE and/or the SMP.
evidence: Supported by stochastic labeling data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The two local SEZ neurons were GABAergic, expressing the VGAT vesicular transporter for GABA.
source: We found that the two local SEZ neurons were GABAergic, expressing the VGAT vesicular transporter for GABA; we named them Janu-GABA1 and Janu-GABA2 (Figure 3A–H).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3A–H.

claim: VGAT precisely localized with nearly all Janu-GABA axonal varicosities.
source: VGAT precisely localized with nearly all Janu-GABA axonal varicosities, and did not localize with other Janu neurons.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3A–H.

claim: VGAT did not localize with other Janu neurons.
source: VGAT precisely localized with nearly all Janu-GABA axonal varicosities, and did not localize with other Janu neurons.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3A–H.

claim: Knockdown of VGAT with either of two distinct RNAi transgenes in the Janu neurons decreased water seeking in thirsty animals.
source: Knockdown of VGAT with either of two distinct RNAi transgenes in the Janu neurons decreased water seeking in thirsty animals (Figure 3I; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knockdown of Gad1 in Janu neurons decreased thirsty water seeking.
source: Knockdown of Gad1, encoding the GABA biosynthetic enzyme Glutamic acid decarboxylase 1, in Janu neurons also decreased thirsty water seeking (Figure 3J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3J.

claim: Gad1 knockdown while simultaneously activating the Janu neurons with TrpA1 blocked activation-dependent water seeking.
source: To ask if Janu-GABA neurons were responsible for promoting water seeking when Janu neurons were activated in water replete flies, we knocked down Gad1 while simultaneously activating the Janu neurons with TrpA1. This manipulation blocked activation-dependent water seeking (Figure 3K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3K.

claim: The Janu-GABA neurons promote thirsty water seeking and are capable of driving water seeking in water replete animals.
source: Thus, the Janu-GABA neurons promote thirsty water seeking and are capable of driving water seeking in water replete animals.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the VGAT and Gad1 knockdown experiments.

claim: Gad1 knockdown in Janu neurons had no effect on total water consumption time.
source: Gad1 knockdown in Janu neurons had no effect on total water consumption time, but it reduced the length of the first intake bout (Figure 3L,M).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3L,M.

claim: Gad1 knockdown in Janu neurons reduced the length of the first intake bout.
source: Gad1 knockdown in Janu neurons had no effect on total water consumption time, but it reduced the length of the first intake bout (Figure 3L,M).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3L,M.

claim: Pharyngeal pumping rate was unchanged in thirsty Janu neuron Gad1 knockdown flies.
source: Pharyngeal pumping rate was unchanged in thirsty Janu neuron Gad1 knockdown flies, indicating that total intake and motor behaviors were unaffected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Feeding behavior was unaltered in the Janu Gad1 knockdown flies.
source: Finally, feeding behavior was unaltered in the Janu Gad1 knockdown flies (Figure 3N).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3N.

claim: The Janu-GABA neurons are thirst-driven water seeking inhibitory local interneurons in the SEZ.
source: Thus, the Janu-GABA neurons are thirst-driven water seeking inhibitory local interneurons in the SEZ.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the anatomical and functional characterization.

claim: The Janu-AstA neuron is a bilaterally symmetric interneuron that projects ipsilaterally from the SEZ to the ventral medial SMP.
source: The Janu-AstA neuron is a bilaterally symmetric interneuron that projects ipsilaterally from the SEZ to the ventral medial SMP, and that expresses the neuropeptide AstA (Figure 4A–G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data in Figure 4A–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The Janu-AstA neuron expresses the neuropeptide AstA.
source: The Janu-AstA neuron is a bilaterally symmetric interneuron that projects ipsilaterally from the SEZ to the ventral medial SMP, and that expresses the neuropeptide AstA (Figure 4A–G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4A–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: AstA knockdown in Janu-spGal4 neurons with either of two independent RNAi transgenes reduced thirsty water seeking.
source: AstA knockdown in Janu-spGal4 neurons with either of two independent RNAi transgenes reduced thirsty water seeking (Figure 4H,I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4H,I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Loss-of-function AstA mutant flies showed markedly reduced water seeking, both as a homozygote and when in trans to a small chromosomal deletion at the AstA locus.
source: Moreover, loss-of-function AstA mutant flies showed markedly reduced water seeking, both as a homozygote and when in trans to a small chromosomal deletion at the AstA locus (Figure 4J,K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4J,K.

claim: AstA knockdown while simultaneously activating the Janu neurons with TrpA1 blocked activation-dependent water seeking.
source: To ask if Janu-AstA neurons were responsible for promoting water seeking when Janu neurons were activated in water replete flies, we knocked down AstA while simultaneously activating the Janu neurons with TrpA1. This manipulation blocked activation-dependent water seeking (Figure 4L; Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The Janu-AstA neurons promote thirsty water seeking and are capable of driving seeking in water replete flies.
source: Thus, like Janu-GABA neurons, the Janu-AstA neurons promote thirsty water seeking and are capable of driving seeking in water replete flies.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the AstA knockdown and activation experiments.

claim: There may exist a functional relationship between the Janu-GABA and the Janu-AstA neurons.
source: This finding suggests that there may exist a functional relationship between the Janu-GABA and the Janu-AstA neurons.
evidence: Speculative inference based on similar functional properties.

claim: AstA knockdown in Janu neurons did not affect total water consumption time.
source: AstA knockdown in Janu neurons did not affect total water consumption time, the length of the first intake bout, pharyngeal pumping rate, or intake measured in the open-field assay (Figure 4M,N; Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4M,N and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: AstA knockdown in Janu neurons did not affect the length of the first intake bout.
source: AstA knockdown in Janu neurons did not affect total water consumption time, the length of the first intake bout, pharyngeal pumping rate, or intake measured in the open-field assay (Figure 4M,N; Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4M,N and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: AstA knockdown in Janu neurons did not affect pharyngeal pumping rate.
source: AstA knockdown in Janu neurons did not affect total water consumption time, the length of the first intake bout, pharyngeal pumping rate, or intake measured in the open-field assay (Figure 4M,N; Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4M,N and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: AstA knockdown in Janu neurons did not affect intake measured in the open-field assay.
source: AstA knockdown in Janu neurons did not affect total water consumption time, the length of the first intake bout, pharyngeal pumping rate, or intake measured in the open-field assay (Figure 4M,N; Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4M,N and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: Janu-AstA neurons are required for thirsty water seeking.
source: Thus, Janu-AstA neurons are required for thirsty water seeking, and they promote seeking when activated in water replete flies, but they have no role in water intake.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the AstA knockdown and activation experiments.

claim: Janu-AstA neurons promote seeking when activated in water replete flies.
source: Thus, Janu-AstA neurons are required for thirsty water seeking, and they promote seeking when activated in water replete flies, but they have no role in water intake.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the AstA knockdown and activation experiments.

claim: Janu-AstA neurons have no role in water intake.
source: Thus, Janu-AstA neurons are required for thirsty water seeking, and they promote seeking when activated in water replete flies, but they have no role in water intake.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the intake experiments.

claim: AstA in the Janu neurons inhibits feeding behavior in both well-fed and hungry flies.
source: Interestingly, AstA in the Janu neurons inhibits feeding behavior in both well-fed and hungry flies (Figure 4O; Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4O and Figure 4—figure supplement 1J.

claim: The Janu-AstA neurons oppositely regulate water seeking and feeding behavior.
source: Thus, the Janu-AstA neurons oppositely regulate water seeking and feeding behavior.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the water seeking and feeding behavior experiments.

claim: The Janu-GABA neurons are specific to water-seeking behavior.
source: This is in contrast to the Janu-GABA neurons that are specific to water-seeking behavior.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparing Janu-GABA and Janu-AstA functional properties.

claim: The Janu-GABA1 neurons were selectively activated in thirsty flies.
source: The Janu-GABA1 neurons were selectively activated in thirsty flies; we detected no thirst-dependent activity in any other Janu neurons (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by TRIC calcium indicator data in Figure 5A,B.

claim: No thirst-dependent activity was detected in any Janu neurons other than Janu-GABA1.
source: The Janu-GABA1 neurons were selectively activated in thirsty flies; we detected no thirst-dependent activity in any other Janu neurons (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by TRIC calcium indicator data in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Hunger did not change the activity of any Janu neuron.
source: Moreover, hunger did not change the activity of any Janu neuron (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by TRIC calcium indicator data in Figure 5C.

claim: The Janu-GABA1 neurons selectively increase activity with increasing water deprivation.
source: These data indicate that the Janu-GABA1 neurons selectively increase activity with increasing water deprivation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the TRIC calcium indicator experiments.

claim: Janu>Chrimson flies that were well fed and water replete were attracted to the activation side of the arena.
source: Janu>Chrimson flies that were well fed and water replete were attracted to the activation side of the arena (Figure 5D,E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic positional preference data in Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Flies showed a similar preference for Chrimson activation of the R65D05 pattern that also contains the Janu water seeking neurons.
source: Flies showed a similar preference for Chrimson activation of the R65D05 pattern that also contains the Janu water seeking neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic positional preference data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Water seeking driven by Janu neurons is rewarding.
source: These findings suggest that water seeking driven by Janu neurons is rewarding.
evidence: Inferred from the positional preference experiments.

claim: Moving up a humidity gradient when thirsty may imply impending repletion to the fly, and an end to the negative valence state of thirst.
source: Moving up a humidity gradient when thirsty may imply impending repletion to the fly, and an end to the negative valence state of thirst (Betley et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Janu-AstA presynaptic outputs partially overlapped with NPF in the SMP.
source: Janu-AstA projects to the SMP, where NPF neurons elaborate synaptic endings. Janu-AstA presynaptic outputs partially overlapped with NPF in the SMP (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Synaptic GRASP revealed that Janu-AstA neurons are presynaptic to NPF neurons.
source: Moreover, synaptic GRASP (GFP Reconstitution Across Synaptic Partners) revealed that Janu-AstA neurons are presynaptic to NPF neurons (Figure 6C; Macpherson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by synaptic GRASP data in Figure 6C and citation.

claim: AstA-R2, but not AstA-R1, knockdown decreased thirsty water seeking.
source: AstA-R2, but not AstA-R1, knockdown decreased thirsty water seeking, and also increased feeding behavior, similar to AstA function in the Janu-AstA neurons (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: AstA-R2 knockdown in NPF neurons increased feeding behavior.
source: AstA-R2, but not AstA-R1, knockdown decreased thirsty water seeking, and also increased feeding behavior, similar to AstA function in the Janu-AstA neurons (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: AstA-R2 knockdown in NPF neurons reduced both total water consumption time and the duration of the first intake bout.
source: AstA-R2 knockdown in NPF neurons, however, reduced both total water consumption time and the duration of the first intake bout, indicating that AstA signaling to NPF neurons affects both water seeking and water ingestion (Figure 6E,F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6E,F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: AstA signaling to NPF neurons affects both water seeking and water ingestion.
source: AstA-R2 knockdown in NPF neurons, however, reduced both total water consumption time and the duration of the first intake bout, indicating that AstA signaling to NPF neurons affects both water seeking and water ingestion (Figure 6E,F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the AstA-R2 knockdown experiments.

claim: Increased water seeking was observed in flies completely lacking NPF.
source: Consistent with AstA-R2 functioning as an inhibitory receptor in NPF neurons, we observed increased water seeking in flies completely lacking NPF and in flies with NPF knocked down in NPF neurons (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6G,H.

claim: Increased water seeking was observed in flies with NPF knocked down in NPF neurons.
source: Consistent with AstA-R2 functioning as an inhibitory receptor in NPF neurons, we observed increased water seeking in flies completely lacking NPF and in flies with NPF knocked down in NPF neurons (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6G,H.

claim: Only two NPF neurons, the P1 neurons and the L1-L neurons, showed any activity, and they both increased activity in thirsty flies.

claim: NPF neurons respond to thirst.
source: These findings indicate that NPF neurons respond to thirst and that NPF neurons receive AstA signals via AstA-R2 to reciprocally regulate thirst and hunger behaviors.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the NPF neuron activity and receptor knockdown experiments.

claim: NPF neurons receive AstA signals via AstA-R2 to reciprocally regulate thirst and hunger behaviors.
source: These findings indicate that NPF neurons respond to thirst and that NPF neurons receive AstA signals via AstA-R2 to reciprocally regulate thirst and hunger behaviors.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the anatomical and functional experiments.

claim: Flies rapidly detect humidity gradients via humid-sensing (Ir68a receptor) and dry-sensing (Ir40a receptor) hygrosensory neurons that are housed in the sacculus on the antennae.
source: Flies rapidly detect humidity gradients via humid-sensing (Ir68a receptor) and dry-sensing (Ir40a receptor) hygrosensory neurons that are housed in the sacculus on the antennae (Enjin et al., 2016; Ji and Zhu, 2015; Knecht et al., 2016; Knecht et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The hygrosensory neurons project to dedicated glomeruli in the antennal lobe, where they synapse onto second order projection neurons to send information to the mushroom bodies, lateral horn, and broadly to other areas of the protocerebrum.
source: The hygrosensory neurons project to dedicated glomeruli in the antennal lobe, where they synapse onto second order projection neurons to send information to the mushroom bodies, lateral horn, and broadly to other areas of the protocerebrum (Frank et al., 2017; Marin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Water taste is facilitated by water-sensing (PPK28 mechanoreceptor) gustatory neurons.
source: Water taste is facilitated by water-sensing (PPK28 mechanoreceptor) gustatory neurons; taste is critical for water consumption in thirsty flies (Cameron et al., 2010; Lau et al., 2017).

claim: Taste is critical for water consumption in thirsty flies.
source: Water taste is facilitated by water-sensing (PPK28 mechanoreceptor) gustatory neurons; taste is critical for water consumption in thirsty flies (Cameron et al., 2010; Lau et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A pair of interoceptive SEZ neurons (ISN) that detect osmolarity are located in the suboesophageal ganglion zone (SEZ).
source: A pair of interoceptive SEZ neurons (ISN) that detect osmolarity are located in the suboesophageal ganglion zone (SEZ); they promote water consumption and reciprocally inhibit food intake when inhibited by high interstitial fluid osmolarity (Jourjine et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ISN neurons promote water consumption and reciprocally inhibit food intake when inhibited by high interstitial fluid osmolarity.
source: A pair of interoceptive SEZ neurons (ISN) that detect osmolarity are located in the suboesophageal ganglion zone (SEZ); they promote water consumption and reciprocally inhibit food intake when inhibited by high interstitial fluid osmolarity (Jourjine et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The ISNs are regulated by the mechanoreceptor Nanchung that responds to changes in hemolymph osmolarity to signal water balance status.
source: The ISNs are regulated by the mechanoreceptor Nanchung that responds to changes in hemolymph osmolarity to signal water balance status, and by adipokinetic hormone that signals aspects of energy store status to the brain.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jourjine et al., 2016 in the previous sentence.

claim: The ISNs are regulated by adipokinetic hormone that signals aspects of energy store status to the brain.
source: The ISNs are regulated by the mechanoreceptor Nanchung that responds to changes in hemolymph osmolarity to signal water balance status, and by adipokinetic hormone that signals aspects of energy store status to the brain.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jourjine et al., 2016 in the previous sentence.

claim: Functional mapping of water reward memories led to the discovery of leucokinin peptidergic neurons, whose activity is regulated by thirst.
source: Functional mapping of water reward memories led to the discovery of leucokinin peptidergic neurons, whose activity is regulated by thirst, and that regulate memories of thirst through dopaminergic connections into the mushroom body learning and memory circuitry (Ji and Zhu, 2015; Lin et al., 2014; Senapati et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Leucokinin peptidergic neurons regulate memories of thirst through dopaminergic connections into the mushroom body learning and memory circuitry.
source: Functional mapping of water reward memories led to the discovery of leucokinin peptidergic neurons, whose activity is regulated by thirst, and that regulate memories of thirst through dopaminergic connections into the mushroom body learning and memory circuitry (Ji and Zhu, 2015; Lin et al., 2014; Senapati et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Thirsty attraction to humidity may also route through some of the same dopamine neurons.
source: Thirsty attraction to humidity may also route through some of the same dopamine neurons (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Hunger is conveyed through dopamine neurons and the mushroom body circuitry.
source: Hunger, which drives a pattern of ingestive behaviors similar to that of thirst, is also conveyed through dopamine neurons and the mushroom body circuitry (Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The pars intercerebralis contains ion transport peptide (ITP) hormone expressing neurons.
source: Finally, the pars intercerebralis, a neuroendocrine brain region, contains ion transport peptide (ITP) hormone expressing neurons (Gáliková et al., 2018; Nässel and Vanden Broeck, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ion transport peptide bidirectionally controls thirst and hunger behaviors.
source: Ion transport peptide bidirectionally controls thirst and hunger behaviors, and it regulates water balance in the body as a hormone.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gáliková et al., 2018 and Nässel and Vanden Broeck, 2016 in the previous sentence.

claim: Ion transport peptide regulates water balance in the body as a hormone.
source: Ion transport peptide bidirectionally controls thirst and hunger behaviors, and it regulates water balance in the body as a hormone.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gáliková et al., 2018 and Nässel and Vanden Broeck, 2016 in the previous sentence.

claim: Thirst can override hunger drive (dehydration-anorexia).
source: For example, thirst can override hunger drive (dehydration-anorexia), and feeding induces thirst (prandial thirst) (Watts and Boyle, 2010).

claim: Feeding induces thirst (prandial thirst).
source: For example, thirst can override hunger drive (dehydration-anorexia), and feeding induces thirst (prandial thirst) (Watts and Boyle, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Manipulation of either cortical or hindbrain neurons in mice can simultaneously impact both hunger and thirst driven ingestive behavior.
source: Manipulation of either cortical or hindbrain neurons in mice can simultaneously impact both hunger and thirst driven ingestive behavior (Eiselt et al., 2021; Gong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Thirst-driven water anticipation and subsequent intake changes the activity of a remarkably broad set of neurons throughout the mouse brain, in a manner that is time-locked to specific behavioral steps.
source: Moreover, thirst-driven water anticipation and subsequent intake changes the activity of a remarkably broad set of neurons throughout the mouse brain, in a manner that is time-locked to specific behavioral steps (Allen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Flies exhibit hunger:thirst and hunger:sleep interdependencies with apparently equivalent ethological relationships.
source: Flies, exhibiting hunger:thirst and hunger:sleep interdependencies with apparently equivalent ethological relationships, will be useful for elaborating circuit motifs for behavioral state interactions, particularly at the level of individual neurons (Melnattur and Shaw, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The Janu-GABA neurons are functionally distinct from the Fdg local interneurons that are also located in the SEZ.
source: The Janu-GABA neurons are functionally distinct from the Fdg local interneurons that are also located in the SEZ (Flood et al., 2013; Pool et al., 2014).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparing functional properties, supported by citations.

claim: The Fdg neurons increase intake of liquid food and promote proboscis extension.
source: The Fdg neurons increase intake of liquid food and promote proboscis extension, behavioral functions we did not observe for the Janu-GABA neurons.
evidence: Supported by citations to Flood et al., 2013 and Pool et al., 2014 in the previous sentence.

claim: The Fdg neurons may also promote water seeking.
source: We showed that the Fdg neurons may also promote water seeking.
evidence: Inferred from the NP883 activation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The Janu-GABA neurons may function upstream or downstream of the osmosensory ISN neurons.
source: We speculate that the Janu-GABA neurons may function upstream or downstream of the osmosensory ISN neurons that, when inhibited, promote water intake (Jourjine et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculative inference supported by citation.

claim: Janu-GABA neuron activation in the SEZ is predicted to lead to inhibition of SEZ neurons, perhaps to repress competing behavioral states represented in the SEZ.
source: Janu-GABA neuron activation in the SEZ is predicted to lead to inhibition of SEZ neurons, perhaps to repress competing behavioral states represented in the SEZ.
evidence: Speculative inference based on GABAergic nature of the neurons.

claim: The Janu-GABA neurons may repress repressor neurons of thirsty seeking, that remain to be identified.
source: Alternatively, the Janu-GABA neurons may repress repressor neurons of thirsty seeking, that remain to be identified.
evidence: Speculative inference about circuit mechanism.

claim: Tonic release of neuropeptides can tune neural circuit function, including the peptidergic modulation of hunger.
source: This lack of response may indicate a tonic role for AstA in feeding and thirst. Tonic release of neuropeptides can tune neural circuit function, including the peptidergic modulation of hunger (Fu et al., 2004; Tu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Peptidergic signaling can be tuned by changing the amount of the receptor in the receiving neuron, as was demonstrated for sensory tuning by the short-NPF (sNPF) neuropeptide.
source: Peptidergic signaling can also be tuned by changing the amount of the receptor in the receiving neuron, as was demonstrated for sensory tuning by the short-NPF (sNPF) neuropeptide (Root et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Janu-GABA and Janu-AstA may work in series in the same circuit, or in parallel in separate circuits that converge, to control thirsty-seeking behaviors.
source: Janu-GABA and Janu-AstA may work in series in the same circuit, or in parallel in separate circuits that converge, to control thirsty-seeking behaviors.
evidence: Speculative inference about circuit organization.

claim: NPF is well studied in Drosophila and in vertebrates as a promoter of feeding behavior.
source: NPF is well studied in Drosophila and in vertebrates as a promoter of feeding behavior – our work indicates a reciprocal role for NPF in thirst behavior (Chen et al., 2019; Luquet et al., 2005; Pool and Scott, 2014; Shen and Cai, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NPF has a reciprocal role in thirst behavior.
source: NPF is well studied in Drosophila and in vertebrates as a promoter of feeding behavior – our work indicates a reciprocal role for NPF in thirst behavior (Chen et al., 2019; Luquet et al., 2005; Pool and Scott, 2014; Shen and Cai, 2001).

claim: Janu-AstA and AstA-R2-positive NPF neurons join a small list of neurons that oppositely regulate thirst and hunger behaviors.
source: Janu-AstA and AstA-R2-positive NPF neurons join a small list of neurons that oppositely regulate thirst and hunger behaviors: the osmosensory ISN neurons oppositely regulate food and water intake, and Ion Transport Peptide (ITP) neurons promote thirst and inhibit food intake (Gáliková et al., 2018; Pool et al., 2014).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from this study and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The osmosensory ISN neurons oppositely regulate food and water intake.
source: Janu-AstA and AstA-R2-positive NPF neurons join a small list of neurons that oppositely regulate thirst and hunger behaviors: the osmosensory ISN neurons oppositely regulate food and water intake, and Ion Transport Peptide (ITP) neurons promote thirst and inhibit food intake (Gáliková et al., 2018; Pool et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ion Transport Peptide (ITP) neurons promote thirst and inhibit food intake.

evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hunger selectively increases the activity of the P1 and L1-l NPF neurons.

source: A potential mechanism may be through NPF-NPF neuronal synapses: both the P1 and the L1-l neurons express the NPF receptor NPFR (Shao et al., 2017).

claim: The Janu neurons likely do not encode the state of deprivation.
